metadata.title: A Survey on Quantum Computational Finance for Derivatives Pricing and VaR
metadata.venue: Archives of Computational Methods in Engineering

problem_domains.problem: pricing of financial derivatives
problem_domains.description: The paper focuses on computing the fair value of derivative contracts such as options, including European, American, and basket options.
problem_domains.quote: In this article, the set of algorithms to be explored corresponds to the pricing of financial derivatives and Value-at-Risk (VaR) computation.

problem_domains.problem: Value-at-Risk (VaR) computation
problem_domains.description: The paper addresses the problem of forecasting portfolio losses via VaR as a key risk measure.
problem_domains.quote: In the second case, the VaR is a risk measure so that the objective is to forecast the losses of future operations.

problem_domains.problem: derivative risk management
problem_domains.description: The paper considers risk management of derivatives, including portfolio risk metrics such as VaR and CVaR.
problem_domains.quote: In the second part of Sect. 2, financial risk management concepts are covered such as Market Risk and Credit Portfolio Management, as well as key risk portfolio metrics such as Value-at-Risk and Conditional Value-at-Risk (or Expected Shortfall).

problem_domains.problem: pricing of European options
problem_domains.description: The paper details the problem of computing fair values for European vanilla call and put options under stochastic models.
problem_domains.quote: For vanilla options, the payoffs only depend on the value of the underlying at expiry date T.
problem_domains.location: Page 4, Section 2.1.1 Financial Derivatives and Options

problem_domains.problem: pricing of American options
problem_domains.description: The paper treats the valuation of American options, which include early exercise features and lead to optimal stopping problems.
problem_domains.quote: In the case of American options, the early exercise opportunity implies the replacement of the PDE problem (10) by a linear complementarity problem associated to the Black-Scholes differential operator:

problem_domains.problem: pricing of basket options
problem_domains.description: The paper discusses options whose payoff depends on multiple underlying assets, increasing dimensionality.
problem_domains.quote: Options that depend on a set of assets are also traded in the financial markets and are known as basket options.

problem_domains.problem: high-dimensional derivatives pricing (curse of dimensionality)
problem_domains.description: The paper highlights computational challenges when pricing derivatives with many underlying assets or factors.
problem_domains.quote: the “curse of dimensionality”, that arises when the number of underlying assets or stochastic factors becomes large.

problem_domains.problem: portfolio credit risk and loss distribution estimation
problem_domains.description: The paper addresses modeling and simulating portfolio credit losses for many counterparties to compute risk measures.
problem_domains.quote: As the credit quality of the counterparty (captured by the asset value in the Merton model) is correlated, this problem is closely related to the basket option covered earlier, but with the additional complexity of having different barriers.

problem_domains.problem: dimensionality reduction in credit portfolio models
problem_domains.description: The paper discusses the need to reduce dimensionality in large credit portfolios using factor models and PCA.
problem_domains.quote: Given its complexity and high dimensionality, credit portfolio modelling relies on dimensionality reduction techniques such as factor models and Principal Component Analysis (PCA).

problem_domains.problem: estimation of VaR and CVaR from loss distributions
problem_domains.description: The paper defines and focuses on computing VaR and CVaR as tail-based risk measures from portfolio loss distributions.
problem_domains.quote: We consider two well-known measures of risk, the Value-at-Risk (VaR) and the Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) (also known as Expected Shortfall).
problem_domains.location: Page 8, Section 2.2 Risk Measures for Derivatives Portfolios

problem_domains.problem: slow convergence of classical Monte Carlo for pricing and risk
problem_domains.description: The paper notes that classical Monte Carlo has O(1/√M) convergence, which is slow for many applications.
problem_domains.quote: Therefore, the quadratic error of the Monte Carlo estimate tends to zero with order O(1∕√M) when M tends to infinity, which is considered slow for many applications.

problem_domains.problem: VaR and CVaR estimation
problem_domains.description: Estimation of Value at Risk and Conditional Value at Risk from loss distributions, especially in high-confidence tail regimes where Monte Carlo is inefficient.
problem_domains.quote: The VaR (and the CVaR) are intended to prevent extreme events of big losses, so the quantile /u1D6FC is usually between 95% and 99.9% depending on the application. In such regimes, Monte Carlo is rather inefficient, specially for the CVaR computation, since the number of samples in the area of interest is usually not sufficient to provide an acceptable precision.
problem_domains.location: Page 11, paragraph starting 'The VaR (and the CVaR) are intended...'

problem_domains.problem: High-dimensional Monte Carlo for pricing and risk
problem_domains.description: Computation of expectation values for pricing and risk problems over high-dimensional domains where classical Monte Carlo becomes costly.
problem_domains.quote: As we saw in Sects. 2.1.3 and 2.2.3, the computation of expectation values constitutes the basis for many pricing and risk problems. Such a computation is normally performed by means of classical Monte Carlo methods. The exponential growth of the dimension of the Hilbert space with the number of qubits, however, suggests that an alternative quantum implementation for Monte Carlo could be in a better position than its classical counterparts, especially over domains with a high dimensionality.
problem_domains.location: Page 12, first full paragraph under 3.1 Quantum‑Accelerated Monte Carlo

problem_domains.problem: Option pricing as expectation of payoff
problem_domains.description: Pricing of (including path-dependent) options formulated as computing the expected value of a payoff function under a risk-neutral probability distribution.
problem_domains.quote: As presented in Eq. (8 ), the option pricing problem can be formulated as the computation of the expected value of a payoff function with respect to a probability distribution:10
problem_domains.location: Page 14, start of 3.1.3 Applications to Option Pricing

problem_domains.problem: Tail risk estimation for portfolios (VaR/CVaR)
problem_domains.description: Risk analysis requiring precise estimation of the tail of loss distributions for portfolios of derivatives, which is demanding for Monte Carlo.
problem_domains.quote: Nevertheless, risk analysis problems require a precise estimation of the tail of a distribution, which constitute a more demanding task in terms of Monte Carlo samplings. On top of that, the problem usually is highly dimensional, because portfolios of various derivatives are usually considered.
problem_domains.location: Page 15, first full paragraph under 3.1.4 Applications to Risk Analysis

problem_domains.problem: Computing probability of large losses and corresponding VaR level
problem_domains.description: Estimating the probability of losses exceeding a threshold and determining the maximal loss corresponding to a given confidence level.
problem_domains.quote: In risk assessment, one can be interested in estimating the probability of experiencing a future loss exceeding a predetermined value, according to, for example, the definition of the VaR and the CVaR risk measures as in Sect. 2.2. Such a question can again be addressed by means of a comparator. More often, one is interested in fixing a (high) confidence level /u1D6FC and asking which maximal loss corresponds to it.
problem_domains.location: Page 15, paragraph starting 'In risk assessment, one can be interested...'

problem_domains.problem: Solving Black–Scholes and related financial PDEs
problem_domains.description: Numerical solution of Black–Scholes-type partial differential equations for derivative pricing, including mapping them to forms amenable to quantum simulation.
problem_domains.quote: Following [36], the quantum approaches rely on the observation that the financial PDEs can be mapped into the propagation governed by an appropriate Hamiltonian operator.
problem_domains.location: Page 16, first paragraph under 3.2 Quantum PDEs

problem_domains.problem: Principal Component Analysis for risk and pricing models
problem_domains.description: Dimensionality reduction of covariance structures in pricing and risk models via PCA.
problem_domains.quote: Principal Component Analysis is a classical mathematical technique that is widely used in quantitative finance for dimensionality reduction; not only for both pricing problems (as Sect.  2.1.1) and in risk models (as the ones in Sect.  2.2.2), but also for stock value forecasting (usually in combination with other machine learning techniques).
problem_domains.location: Page 11, paragraph starting 'Principal Component Analysis is a classical...'

problem_domains.problem: Eigen-decomposition of covariance matrices for PCA
problem_domains.description: Computing eigenvalues and eigenvectors of large, dense covariance matrices used in financial PCA.
problem_domains.quote: The first step behind PCA is to calculate the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix Σ∈ℝ N × ℝN , which is Hermitian and positive semi-definite.
problem_domains.location: Page 18, first paragraph under 3.3.1 Quantum Principal Component Analysis

problem_domains.problem: Regression-based pricing, especially for early-exercise options
problem_domains.description: Using regression and linear system solving in Monte Carlo pricing of options with early exercise such as American options.
problem_domains.quote: Classical and more advanced (neural networks-based) regression methodologies are greatly appreciated in derivative pricing problems, in particular for options with early exercise, like American options (see Sect.  2.1.1), when they are priced by Monte Carlo methods.

problem_domains.problem: Deep learning for PDEs, BSDEs, and other finance tasks
problem_domains.description: Application of deep neural networks to solve PDEs, BSDEs, inverse option pricing, and counterparty credit risk.
problem_domains.quote: As it is the case for many other disciplines, computational finance greatly benefits from this new computational paradigm, with successful developments on numerical solutions for PDEs or Backward Stochastic Differential Equations (BSDE), inverse option pricing problems, counterparty credit risk computations, etc.
problem_domains.location: Page 19, paragraph under 3.3.3 Quantum Neural Networks and Deep Learning

problem_domains.problem: Loading probability distributions for pricing and VaR
problem_domains.description: Efficiently constructing a quantum circuit that loads a given probability distribution over scenarios or paths, which is required for QAMC in pricing and VaR.
problem_domains.quote: The main implicit assumption in QAMC is the existence of an efficient oracle which loads the probability distribution. Both for pricing and VaR, loading the distribution means that it is necessary to create a circuit for a unitary operation P such that:

problem_domains.problem: Simulation of SDEs for pricing distributions
problem_domains.description: Generating the underlying probability distribution for pricing via simulation of stochastic differential equations, which dominates classical computational cost.
problem_domains.quote: In pricing, the distribution to be loaded has to be previously generated through the simulation of a SDE. As it was discussed in the first part of this survey, the simulation of the SDE consumes most of the computing resources.
problem_domains.location: Page 20, paragraph starting 'In pricing, the distribution to be loaded...'

problem_domains.problem: VaR problems
problem_domains.description: The survey discusses how loading probability distributions into quantum states directly benefits Value-at-Risk calculations, which require empirical distributions.
problem_domains.quote: 1. Loading a probability distribution: the direct benefits in this matter goes to VaR problems.

problem_domains.problem: Loading empirical distributions for VaR
problem_domains.description: VaR calculations always require loading an empirical probability distribution into the quantum register, making state loading a key bottleneck.
problem_domains.quote: As opposed to pricing where there are cases in which the probability distribution can be generated sinthetically, in VaR we always need to load an empirical distribution. Thus, the loading step is of particular importance for VaR.

problem_domains.problem: Pricing (derivatives pricing)
problem_domains.description: The survey treats pricing problems where payoff functions must be loaded and probability distributions may be generated synthetically or via stochastic simulation.
problem_domains.quote: 3. Loading a payoff function: this case is only relevant for pricing.

problem_domains.problem: Simulation of stochastic differential equations for underlying assets
problem_domains.description: The document frames the need to simulate discrete stochastic processes that approximate SDEs for underlying assets, especially when no analytical solution exists or options are path dependent.
problem_domains.quote: With “generative approach” we refer to the actual simulation of the discrete stochastic processes which generate the desired approximate distribution. The discrete stochastic approach is particularly important when the underlying asset SDE does not admit an analytical formulation, or when the option is path dependent (thus requiring the knowledge of the distribution of the underlying at intermediate times before maturity) as it usually happens in pricing.

problem_domains.problem: Loading payoff functions for options
problem_domains.description: The survey highlights the challenge of loading payoff functions, especially arbitrary or non-piecewise-linear payoffs, into quantum circuits for expectation value computation.
problem_domains.quote: The task of computing the expectation value of a payoff  function with respect to a probability distribution, see Eq. (53), requires that both be loaded into the quantum circuit, accordingly to the pipeline depicted in Fig. 2.

problem_domains.problem: Implementation of payoff functions for European vanilla options and piecewise linear payoffs
problem_domains.description: The paper notes that European vanilla option payoffs are relatively easy to implement via comparator circuits, but general piecewise linear payoffs already increase circuit complexity.
problem_domains.quote: The payoff functions for European vanilla options, see Eq. (1), are relatively easy to implement by means of a comparator circuit. As long as the payoff function is piecewise linear, one can generalize the approach implemented for the European vanilla contracts. Nonetheless, this would already entail an increased level of complexity in the quantum circuit; for instance, any separation point between two linear regions would require a comparator circuit19.

problem_domains.problem: General arbitrary payoff loading
problem_domains.description: For arbitrary payoff functions, loading them into a quantum state that already encodes the probability distribution can be more complex than loading the distribution itself.
problem_domains.quote: In a completely general case, i.e. for arbitrary payoff, its loading problem can be even more complicated than that of the probability distribution function.

problem_domains.problem: Derivatives pricing and financial risk management (general)
problem_domains.description: The survey addresses the broader financial problems of derivative pricing and financial risk management, including VaR and PDE-based approaches.
problem_domains.quote: While this progress is very encouraging, further work will be required to prove that Quantum Computing can deliver real-world advantage to the areas of derivative pricing and financial risk management.

problem_domains.problem: Solution of PDEs arising in finance
problem_domains.description: The document discusses solving partial differential equations on quantum computers with applications to derivative pricing and risk management.
problem_domains.quote: An area that is also showing some interesting results is the solution of PDEs using quantum computers with applications to derivative pricing and risk management.

solution_approaches.approach: quantum alternatives to classical Monte Carlo based on Quantum Amplitude Estimation
solution_approaches.description: The paper reviews quantum Monte Carlo-style methods for pricing and VaR that rely on Quantum Amplitude Estimation and its variants.
solution_approaches.quote: Section 3 starts discussing quantum alternatives to classical Monte Carlo. The cornerstone of the quantum alternatives to Monte Carlo rely on Quantum Amplitude Estimation and more modern variations on this technique.

solution_approaches.approach: quantum methods for solving derivative pricing models using PDEs
solution_approaches.description: The paper considers quantum algorithms that tackle PDE-based formulations of derivative pricing problems.
solution_approaches.quote: Later on, still in Sect. 3, quantum methods for solving derivative pricing models using PDEs are also discussed.

solution_approaches.approach: numerical quantum techniques closer to Machine Learning for pricing and VaR
solution_approaches.description: The paper introduces quantum numerical techniques for pricing and VaR that are conceptually related to machine learning approaches.
solution_approaches.quote: In the third block of Sect. 3 we introduce some numerical quantum techniques for pricing and VaR which, at least in spirit, are closer to Machine Learning.

solution_approaches.approach: efficient loading or generation of probability distributions in a quantum computer
solution_approaches.description: The paper identifies efficient quantum state preparation of probability distributions as a key technical component for quantum Monte Carlo-style algorithms.
solution_approaches.quote: Section 3 concludes with a review of the key remaining challenges for quantum alternatives to Monte Carlo to deliver their potential advantage, namely, the efficient loading or generation of probability distributions in a quantum computer and the computation of the payoff functions in pricing problems.

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum-Accelerated Monte Carlo (QAMC)
solution_approaches.description: Quantum algorithms that implement Monte Carlo-style expectation estimation using amplitude amplification and estimation to achieve quadratic precision scaling.
solution_approaches.quote: Quantum-Accelerated Monte Carlo8 for the computation of the expected value of a function is usually divided in four steps (see Fig.  2):

solution_approaches.approach: Amplitude amplification
solution_approaches.description: Use of Grover-style operators to increase the probability of measuring 'good' states corresponding to desired outcomes.
solution_approaches.quote: the amplitude amplification algorithm gives us a strategy to enhance the probability of measuring � ̃Ψ1⟩ , namely the “good” or marked state.

solution_approaches.approach: Original amplitude estimation with inverse Quantum Fourier Transform
solution_approaches.description: Amplitude estimation using controlled Grover iterations and an inverse Quantum Fourier Transform on an auxiliary register.
solution_approaches.quote: The path suggested in the original paper [15] is to adopt an inverse quantum Fourier transform, see Fig.  3.
solution_approaches.location: Page 13, first paragraph under 'Original Amplitude Estimation'

solution_approaches.approach: Amplitude estimation with Max Likelihood
solution_approaches.description: Amplitude estimation avoiding QFT by collecting measurement data for different Grover powers and using classical maximum likelihood post-processing.
solution_approaches.quote: One interesting possibility to avoid the inverse Quantum Fourier transform has been suggested in [84] and it relies on classical post-processing.
solution_approaches.location: Page 13, paragraph under 'Quantum Amplitude Amplification and Estimation with Max Likelihood'

solution_approaches.approach: Iterative Quantum Amplitude Estimation
solution_approaches.description: A variant of amplitude estimation without quantum phase estimation, reducing qubits and gates while maintaining quadratic speed-up.
solution_approaches.quote: In [39] a different variant of quantum amplitude estimation is considered, which does not need quantum phase estimation, that is, it avoids the estimation of /u1D703 through an inverse Quantum Fourier Transform.
solution_approaches.location: Page 13–14, first paragraph under 'Iterative Quantum Amplitude Estimation'

solution_approaches.approach: Power-law amplitude estimation
solution_approaches.description: An amplitude estimation algorithm that optimizes the sampling schedule using a power-law trade-off between total oracle calls and depth.
solution_approaches.quote: The Power-law algorithm (sometimes referred to as Kerenidis-Prakash algorithm) refines the Max Likelihood algorithm of [84].

solution_approaches.approach: QoPrime amplitude estimation
solution_approaches.description: Amplitude estimation based on the Chinese Remainder Theorem, using coprime sampling schedules to combine low-accuracy samples into high-accuracy estimates.
solution_approaches.quote: The QoPrime algorithm follows the same trade-off between N and D as the Power-law algorithm, however its strategy is based on a result from number theory, that is known as Chinese Remainder Theorem.

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum coins
solution_approaches.description: Grover-family algorithms that load the integrand function directly into amplitudes (direct embedding) instead of its square root, avoiding inverse QFT.
solution_approaches.quote: Although belonging to the same family of Grover algorithms, the quantum coin loads the integrand function (and not its square root) into the quantum state amplitude.

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum comparator circuits and binary search for VaR/CVaR
solution_approaches.description: Use of quantum comparator circuits to implement payoff activation or loss thresholds, combined with binary search to find VaR levels.
solution_approaches.quote: Such a question can again be addressed by means of a comparator. More often, one is interested in fixing a (high) confidence level /u1D6FC and asking which maximal loss corresponds to it. This question can be addressed combining a comparator with a binary search algorithm [26, 27].
solution_approaches.location: Page 15, paragraph starting 'In risk assessment, one can be interested...'

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum multi-level Monte Carlo
solution_approaches.description: Quantum generalization of multi-level Monte Carlo where a quantum circuit solves each Monte Carlo sub-problem in a telescopic sum.
solution_approaches.quote: As a final remark on quantum-enhanced Monte Carlo techniques, we refer to [7 ] for the quantum generalization of the classical multi-level Monte Carlo strategy [32].
solution_approaches.location: Page 15, last paragraph under 3.1.4 Applications to Risk Analysis

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum PDEs via Hamiltonian propagation with ĤBS
solution_approaches.description: Mapping Black–Scholes PDE to a Schrödinger-like equation with a non-Hermitian Hamiltonian ĤBS and simulating its propagation using QFT and Cartan decomposition.
solution_approaches.quote: In [36] they consider the Hamiltonian (68) and exploit the fact that it is diagonal in momentum space. Thus, by means of a quantum Fourier transform, and its inverse, they are able to work with a diagonal propagator, which admits an efficient decomposition in the Cartan basis.
solution_approaches.location: Page 17, first paragraph under 3.2.1 Propagating with ̂HBS

solution_approaches.approach: Imaginary-time propagation with ĤHE
solution_approaches.description: Transforming Black–Scholes to a heat equation and then to an imaginary-time Schrödinger equation, solved via variational imaginary-time evolution.
solution_approaches.quote: A quantum algorithm for imaginary-time propagation has been developed in the field of quantum chemistry [63]. 13 It assumes to deal with a Hamiltonian
solution_approaches.location: Page 17, first paragraph under 3.2.2 Imaginary‑Time Propagation with ̂HHE

solution_approaches.approach: Variational imaginary-time evolution (McLachlan principle)
solution_approaches.description: Using a parametrized circuit and McLachlan’s variational principle to evolve parameters according to a linear system and approximate ground states relevant to pricing PDEs.
solution_approaches.quote: More technically, the imaginary-time method entails considering a McLachlan variational principle

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum Principal Component Analysis (QPCA)
solution_approaches.description: Using quantum algorithms to obtain eigenvalues/eigenvectors of covariance matrices treated as density matrices, potentially with exponential speedup.
solution_approaches.quote: Another possibility is to work with the covariance matrix Σ as a density matrix (usually represented as /u1D70C ), and make a Quantum Principal Component Analysis (QPCA).
solution_approaches.location: Page 18, paragraph starting 'Another possibility is to work with the covariance matrix...'

solution_approaches.approach: Variational QPCA via density matrix expansion
solution_approaches.description: Expressing the covariance matrix as a sum over an operator basis and learning a unitary that diagonalizes it using variational hybrid algorithms.
solution_approaches.quote: Recently, [92] suggested to calculate the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of Σ through a variational algorithm, by using the density matrix expansion

solution_approaches.approach: HHL-based quantum regression
solution_approaches.description: Using the HHL algorithm for solving linear systems as a subroutine in quantum regression methods for pricing.
solution_approaches.quote: The HHL algorithm proposed in [43] is a first relevant representative algorithm for solving linear systems, allowing to diagonalize some special matrices with exponential speedup. Then, the HHL algorithm was employed to perform a regression on a quantum computer in [90].

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum kernel estimation and Gaussian process QML
solution_approaches.description: Quantum machine learning approaches such as quantum kernel estimation and Gaussian process models for regression-like tasks.
solution_approaches.quote: Other quantum-based techniques like Quantum Kernel Estimation  [28] and QML with Gaussian processes [94] have been recently proposed.

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum neural networks (QNNs) and deep learning
solution_approaches.description: Fully quantum neural network architectures and training methods, including for function or distribution loading.
solution_approaches.quote: Another research line consists in the algorithms based on a fully Quantum Neural Network (QNN). In the last few years, many works on QNN advanced training have been proposed, among which we highlight [ 10, 23]. One of the main applications of QNNs is the function (or distribution) loading.
solution_approaches.location: Page 19–20, paragraph under 3.3.3 Quantum Neural Networks and Deep Learning

solution_approaches.approach: Grover approach for loading probability distributions
solution_approaches.description: A Grover-based method discretizes a continuous probability density into regions and iteratively maps conditioned probabilities into amplitudes of a quantum state.
solution_approaches.quote: Grover Approach [40] proposed a general methodology to load integrable probability distributions into the states efficiently.

solution_approaches.approach: Variational Quantum Circuits for approximated state loading
solution_approaches.description: Parametric quantum circuits are trained to approximate the amplitudes of a target probability distribution, potentially via QGANs.
solution_approaches.quote: • Variational Quantum Circuits: create an ad-hoc circuit which approximates the amplitudes [68].

solution_approaches.approach: Tensor Networks techniques for state preparation
solution_approaches.description: Tensor network ansatzes, particularly matrix product states, are used to encode amplitude functions efficiently into quantum circuits.
solution_approaches.quote: • Tensor Networks techniques [31, 48, 72].

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum Generative Adversarial Networks (QGANs)
solution_approaches.description: QGANs use a parametric quantum generator circuit trained adversarially to transform an initial distribution into a desired probability distribution for option pricing and other tasks.
solution_approaches.quote: QGANs have been proposed by [75, 95]. They are based on the classical concept proposed by [37], where two deep learning models are trained simultaneously in an adversarial setup.

solution_approaches.approach: Variational quantum simulation via trinomial trees
solution_approaches.description: Variational quantum simulation implements discrete stochastic processes, such as trinomial trees, using ladder operators and linear combinations of unitaries to generate asset price distributions.
solution_approaches.quote: In the class of generative techniques we find the variational quantum simulation [29], implemented—for example—by means of trinomial trees [ 57] (see Sect. 2.1.3)17.

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum walks for generative techniques
solution_approaches.description: Quantum walks are proposed as quantum analogues of classical random walks and multistage Markov chains to generate distributions for risk models and Monte Carlo-like simulations.
solution_approaches.quote: Another interesting member of the class of generative techniques is given by quantum walks [6 , 7, 62, 67]. These can be seen as quantum alternatives to classical Monte Carlo techniques based on multiple-stage Markov chains.

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum Amplitude Estimation (QAE) and Quantum Amplitude Monte Carlo (QAMC)
solution_approaches.description: The survey discusses QAE/QAMC where overall calculation time is dominated by loading the probability distribution, and recent low-depth QAE variants circumvent Quantum Fourier Transform.
solution_approaches.quote: For example, [31, 67] show that in QAMC the overall calculation time is dominated by the (asymptotic) time to load the probability distribution as

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum-inspired tensor network methods for multivariate analysis and PDEs
solution_approaches.description: Tensor network techniques, especially matrix product states, are used in quantum-inspired classical algorithms for multivariate analysis and solving PDEs relevant to finance.
solution_approaches.quote: Tensor network techniques have been studied also in the quantum-inspired realm of classical algorithms. Two relevant example applications are the efficient classical simulation of Shor’s factorization algorithm [25] and generic multivariate analysis [31] (e.g. expected value, Fourier transform, interpolation and solving PDE).

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum Machine Learning (QML) with projected quantum kernels
solution_approaches.description: QML algorithms using projected quantum kernels are proposed to achieve potential quantum advantage in learning tasks related to PDEs and financial models.
solution_approaches.quote: Furthermore, QML algorithms can present some interesting theoretical advantages over their classical counterparts, see for example [49], where the authors introduce the concept of “projected quantum kernel” to show numerical results that promise a quantum advantage in learning algorithms.

problem_solution_mappings.approach: quantum alternatives to classical Monte Carlo based on Quantum Amplitude Estimation
problem_solution_mappings.quote: Section 3 starts discussing quantum alternatives to classical Monte Carlo. The cornerstone of the quantum alternatives to Monte Carlo rely on Quantum Amplitude Estimation and more modern variations on this technique. Despite its relative simplicity, Monte Carlo approaches are widely used for derivative pricing and derivative risk management in financial institutions

problem_solution_mappings.approach: quantum alternatives to classical Monte Carlo based on Quantum Amplitude Estimation
problem_solution_mappings.quote: Despite its relative simplicity, Monte Carlo approaches are widely used for derivative pricing and derivative risk management in financial institutions mainly due to their general purpose and larger resilience to the “curse of dimensionality”, that arises when the number of underlying assets or stochastic factors becomes large.

problem_solution_mappings.approach: Variational Quantum Circuits for approximated state loading
problem_solution_mappings.quote: In order to seek for efficient loading algorithms, we can give up techniques which load the exact function in the quantum state and explore the possibility of approximating the state to be loaded. In this way we lower the resources necessary to load the state at the cost of accuracy and exploit the fact that we are working with a specific subset of functions. This generic idea of loading an approximated version of the state, aiming to have an efficient process, can take different practical paths. We focus on two of them: • Variational Quantum Circuits: create an ad-hoc circuit which approximates the amplitudes [68].

problem_solution_mappings.quote: This generic idea of loading an approximated version of the state, aiming to have an efficient process, can take different practical paths. problem_solution_mappings.approach: Comparator circuits for European vanilla and piecewise linear payoffs
problem_solution_mappings.quote: The payoff functions for European vanilla options, see Eq. (1), are relatively easy to implement by means of a comparator circuit. As long as the payoff function is piecewise linear, one can generalize the approach implemented for the European vanilla contracts.

problem_solution_mappings.approach: Pointwise loading (small examples) and general unitary representations
problem_solution_mappings.quote: For small size examples, the payoff can be loaded pointwise. However this is clearly an approach which scales inefficiently and cannot be planned for real applications.

problem_solution_mappings.problem: Derivatives pricing and financial risk management (general)
problem_solution_mappings.approach: Quantum Amplitude Estimation and related Monte Carlo methods
problem_solution_mappings.quote: Recent achievements in Quantum Amplitude Estimation allow us to circumvent the use of resource-demanding Quantum Fourier Transforms, providing grounds for optimism.

problem_solution_mappings.problem: Solution of PDEs arising in finance
problem_solution_mappings.approach: Quantum algorithms for PDEs and QML-based PDE solvers
problem_solution_mappings.quote: An area that is also showing some interesting results is the solution of PDEs using quantum computers with applications to derivative pricing and risk management. While exciting, these approaches have not yet been able to prove whether quantum algorithms can provide an advantage over their classical counterparts. Lastly, relatively recent advances in both classical and Quantum Machine Learning algorithms for solving PDEs are also exciting, especially because it has been shown that QML can be robust when implemented in noisy hardware.

key_claims.claim: Quantum computing promises faster responses for computationally demanding financial algorithms and can address problems that are currently intractable.
key_claims.quote: For an increasing number of cases, quantum computing promises faster responses that can provide solutions to up-to-now intractable problems.

key_claims.claim: There is no known analytical solution for the American option linear complementarity problem, so numerical methods are required.
key_claims.quote: There is no known analytical solution to this problem and therfore it needs to be solved numerically.

key_claims.claim: Classical Monte Carlo is inefficient for VaR and especially CVaR in high-confidence tail regimes.
key_claims.quote: In such regimes, Monte Carlo is rather inefficient, specially for the CVaR computation, since the number of samples in the area of interest is usually not sufficient to provide an acceptable precision.

key_claims.claim: The inverse Quantum Fourier Transform is a serious bottleneck for original amplitude estimation on near-term devices.
key_claims.quote: The inverse Quantum Fourier transform adopted by the original amplitude estimation algorithm [15] is resource demanding and thus constitutes a serious bottleneck, especially in relation to current or near-future technologies.

key_claims.claim: Quantum PDE approaches based on ĤBS may offer exponential speedup in the propagation subroutine but face open problems in loading models and payoffs.
key_claims.quote: They study the possibility of truncating the Hamiltonian retaining just a polynomial number of interactions and, on this basis, they claim an exponential speedup in the Hamiltonian propagation subroutine. Nevertheless, an overall exponential speedup for the entire pipeline would require efficient loading of the uncertainty model and of the payoff function. These issues remain as open problems.

key_claims.quote: In general, these facts limit the scalability of QPCA to O(N2) operations. However, it could still exhibit better performance than the general classical complexity, which corresponding to O(N3) operations.

key_claims.claim: The main implicit assumption in QAMC is an efficient probability-loading oracle, which is critical and often unrealistic.
key_claims.quote: The main implicit assumption in QAMC is the existence of an efficient oracle which loads the probability distribution.

key_claims.claim: When accounting for SDE simulation and distribution loading, there is no rigorous evidence of quadratic speed-up for QAMC in pricing.
key_claims.quote: Indeed, the claims of a quadratic speed-up of the QAMC over the CMC for financial applications—in general—do not take into account the generation step. If we compare both QAMC and CMC under the same conditions, with the approaches proposed in the literature, we will find that there is no rigorous evidence for the quadratic speed-up.
key_claims.location: Page 20, paragraph starting 'In pricing, the distribution to be loaded...'

key_claims.claim: A quadratic speed-up is not sufficient for practical quantum advantage due to large constant overheads such as error correction.
key_claims.quote: an important (negative) claim has been described in [8], where it is argued that a quadratic speed-up is not sufficient to obtain a quantum advantage, mainly due to the—constant but large—resource overheads (needed for error correction).
key_claims.location: Page 20, paragraph starting 'Many ideal algorithms studied in the literature...'

key_claims.claim: Path-dependent derivatives may be necessary to reach regimes where quantum technologies can provide advantage, but current resource estimates are prohibitive.
key_claims.quote: They argue that the complexity of the pricing task implied by path dependence is a necessary ingredient to find a regime where quantum technologies can lead to an advantage with respect to their classical counterparts. However, the benchmark cases are showed to need 7.5k  logical qubits and a depth of 46 million T-gates and a clock-rate of 10 MHz (current quantum technologies moves on the order of 10 kHz). These are recognized as markedly prohibitive for the moment, yet they set an order-of-magnitude scenario, useful to frame further research and strategy.

key_claims.claim: Loading the probability distribution is often the main bottleneck in quantum amplitude Monte Carlo for finance.
key_claims.quote: Loading the necessary state into a quantum register in order to initialize an algorithm constitutes often the main bottleneck. For example, [31, 67] show that in QAMC the overall calculation time is dominated by the (asymptotic) time to load the probability distribution as

key_claims.claim: General methods to load exact probability distributions have poor scalability with the number of points.
key_claims.quote: The main problem of the first two methods is the poor scalability with the number of points that we need to load.

key_claims.claim: Approximating the quantum state to be loaded can reduce resource requirements at the cost of accuracy.
key_claims.quote: In order to seek for efficient loading algorithms, we can give up techniques which load the exact function in the quantum state and explore the possibility of approximating the state to be loaded. In this way we lower the resources necessary to load the state at the cost of accuracy and exploit the fact that we are working with a specific subset of functions.

key_claims.claim: Grover-based state preparation methods may not yield a speedup for Monte Carlo according to recent works.
key_claims.quote: However, some recent works dispute the possibility of a speed-up when this method is used for Monte Carlo [19, 45, 52].

key_claims.claim: Variational methods lack clear guarantees on loading performance and speed-up due to optimization uncertainty.
key_claims.quote: In general, variational methods do not provide a clear path to get the sought for speed-up. Specifically, it is difficult to guarantee the loading performance by means of rigorous bounds. This is mainly due to the uncertainty associated to the optimization of the parameters [19].

key_claims.claim: Tensor network techniques offer promising, efficient, and scalable encoding of amplitude functions but extension to general empirical distributions is not yet known.
key_claims.quote: Matrix product states (MPS) constitute a widely used class of tensor network ansatzes. These have been long studied in the context of quantum computation [76] and have been recently claimed to allow for an efficient and scalable encoding of explicit amplitude functions with a high fidelity, relying just on linear-depth quantum circuits [48]. ... Although being a promising method, the extension to a general empirical data-based probability is not, to our knowledge, yet known and needs further research.

key_claims.claim: Loading arbitrary payoff functions can be more complicated than loading probability distributions and scales inefficiently if done pointwise.
key_claims.quote: In a completely general case, i.e. for arbitrary payoff, its loading problem can be even more complicated than that of the probability distribution function. ... For small size examples, the payoff can be loaded pointwise. However this is clearly an approach which scales inefficiently and cannot be planned for real applications.

key_claims.claim: Further work is required to demonstrate real-world quantum advantage in derivative pricing and financial risk management, especially on NISQ devices.
key_claims.quote: While this progress is very encouraging, further work will be required to prove that Quantum Computing can deliver real-world advantage to the areas of derivative pricing and financial risk management. Especially if this advantage is to be delivered on Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum technology with limitations to both the number of logical qubits and the width of quantum circuits.

key_claims.claim: Efficient methods for loading probability distributions and representing payoff functions as unitaries are still needed.
key_claims.quote: Further theoretical work is needed in order to find efficient (ideally optimal) ways to load probability distributions to quantum registers, as well as efficient mathematical representations of payoff functions using unitary transforms that can be easily implemented in a quantum circuit.

key_claims.claim: Quantum algorithms for PDEs in finance have not yet demonstrated an advantage over classical methods.
key_claims.quote: While exciting, these approaches have not yet been able to prove whether quantum algorithms can provide an advantage over their classical counterparts.

key_claims.claim: QML can be robust on noisy hardware and projected quantum kernels may offer quantum advantage in learning, but real-world problems remain too high-dimensional for classical handling.
key_claims.quote: Lastly, relatively recent advances in both classical and Quantum Machine Learning algorithms for solving PDEs are also exciting, especially because it has been shown that QML can be robust when implemented in noisy hardware. Furthermore, QML algorithms can present some interesting theoretical advantages over their classical counterparts, see for example [49], where the authors introduce the concept of “projected quantum kernel” to show numerical results that promise a quantum advantage in learning algorithms. These kernels work by projecting the quantum states to an approximate classical representation, helping to reduce the dimensionality of the problem, however for real-world examples the dimension would be still too large to be handled efficiently using a classical computer.

key_claims.claim: Research into financial applications of quantum computing is accelerating, but important breakthroughs across the technology stack are still needed.
key_claims.quote: In summary, research into financial applications of quantum computing is accelerating with new ideas emerging at rapid pace and while important breakthroughs across the technology stack will be needed to make the approach viable, the recent accelerated publication of important results is encouraging.

open_questions.question: How can full quantum algorithms for pricing and VaR be designed so that subroutine speed-ups translate into end-to-end quantum advantage?
open_questions.quote: These problems provide concrete examples about possible issues encountered in designing full quantum algorithms able to reach a quantum advantage. Almost any speed-up concentrated in a subroutine of an overarching inefficient algorithm, however interesting, is clearly not sufficient to reach quantum advantage.

open_questions.question: What are realistic thresholds for quantum advantage in finance when considering not only time complexity but also energy consumption and cost?

This is only a part of a bigger picture which needs to involve other variables such as the energy consumption and cost. Strangely enough, this wider picture is usually not analyzed in the quantum finance literature.
